newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire refugee camp deserted but for rats and bodies.
newsitem.headline: Zaire refugee camp deserted but for rats and bodies.

text.p: Swarms of rats reclaimed the world's largest refugee camp on Friday as hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutus abandoned their hovels, leaving behind the debris of two years in exile in Zaire as well as the freshly mutilated bodies of women and children.

Suddenly and against all expectations Mugunga camp emptied itself within hours as, according to U.N. estimates, up to 700,000 refugees began the short trek back to Rwanda from the Goma border area of eastern Zaire.

The refugees were finally able to leave after the feared Hutu Interahamwe militia and ex-government soldiers fled deeper into Zaire, pursued by Zairean rebels. The Hutu fighters had made Mugunga their base after the 1994 genocide of Rwanda's Tutsi minority and their subsequent defeat by Tutsi forces.
Before dawn the Hutu refugees gathered their few possessions, crossed the front line and set off eastwards to an uncertain future.

"In one area near the Oxfam water tanks we discovered 26 dead people, all women and children apart from one man, macheted to death with their heads split open. Camps are virtually deserted and tens of thousands of rats are reclaiming the camps," U.N. refugee agency spokesman Ray Wilkinson told reporters in Goma.
Reporters saw 13 more bodies in a ditch by the road to Goma.

In one group lay the bloated corpse of a beheaded woman with both arms chopped off. She was naked on top of a pile of seven bodies, jumbled amongst a collection of suitcases, shoes, mattresses and clothing.
Refugees told reporters that Tutsi rebels had killed the refugees but it was also possible that Hutu militiamen who had intimidated the refugees into staying in Zaire had slaughtered them.
By mid-afternoon from Mugunga camp to the outskirts of Goma town, a distance of some eight km (five miles), the road was blocked by hundreds of thousands of refugees, walking 10 abreast.
Almost all were healthy and walking steadily.

There were over 700,000 Rwandan Hutus in camps in the Goma region before the start of the rebellion over a month ago by Zairean Tutsis opposed to both President Mobutu Sese Seko and the presence of the Hutu refugees.
"There could be the total population of the camps moving towards Rwanda," said Ray Wilkinson of the U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR).

"The impasse has been broken. People are moving in the right direction. This is amazing and unstoppable and is not a replay of 1994 because very few of these people seem to be ill and there are no reports of any dead people yet," he said inside Mugunga camp.
It was burnt, looted and ransacked.
The ground was littered with discarded paper, medical kits and hundreds of dead rats.
Six hours of bombardment around the camp on Thursday by the Tutsi rebels who are close to Rwanda's new government seemed to have been the last straw for the Hutu fighters.
The refugees knew the rebels still had days to pile on the pressure before a proposed multinational force pitched up.
"We all fled because of the fighting yesterday," said Vincent Nzehsi. "I am going back to Rubavu, Rwanda. There are no militia in the camp, they are all in the forest."
"They tried to get us to stay but all of us left the camp and are going home to Rwanda," said Jean-Marie Vianna, pushing a bicycle and holding a flapping turkey by its neck.
Refugees said the Interahamwe had moved to forests west of Mugunga. The militiamen know they face execution or years in prison if they return to Rwanda.
By afternoon the vanguard of refugees was crossing the border. Aid agencies, overwhelmed by such an exodus, were desperately trying to shelter and feed them.
"We've very pleased this has happened. It's been a rush but we've got food and aid coming," said Stefano Severe, the UNHCR delegate in Goma.
